rv.q: With the life struggles of his homeland, climate, economically and physically, the lack of resources, famine, money, and education, he sees something that everyone else around him can’t. The power to make something to make change. Those around him laugh, question, and doubt his gathering of scrap that he finds, yet it doesn’t deter him.

With a famine on the horizon and limited access to water for crop irrigation, William believes the secret to salvation lies in being able to pull his village out of energy poverty with a homemade wind turbine. But this is a tale not just about the realisation of William’s scientific ambitions: it is also the story of a community.
The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind is incredibly rich and uplifting.

Guided by scraps of knowledge and a sympathetic librarian, he begins to imagine a windmill that could generate electricity and save his community from famine. It is a compelling premise, and Richy Hughes’ book and lyrics ensure that the stakes are always clear.

In many ways, @sohoplace is the perfect venue for The Boy The Wind: the intimate thrust staging is perfect for elaborate ensemble choreography and carousing the audience. This new musical, based on the memoir and film of the same name, is at its heart a story about community, and it works if we feel as immersed in that community as possible.
